title: Acid-free materials: what they are and how to choose them
subtitle: Understanding pH levels, lignin, and buffering in archival scrapbooking materials
excerpt: Acid-free is printed on almost every scrapbooking product, but what it means and how important it is varies considerably between materials. Paper, adhesives, decorative elements, and protective sleeves all have different acid-related risks. Understanding which materials truly need to be archival quality and which ones are only in contact with copies rather than originals is the most useful knowledge for a scrapbooker buying materials.
sourceNotes: Archival materials science for scrapbooking draws on conservation chemistry and library science standards. The American Library Association and the Smithsonian Institution have both published public-domain guidance on acid-free paper standards and the permanence of archival materials.

glossaryTerms.definition: Paper with a pH of 7.0 or higher at the time of manufacture. Acid causes paper cellulose to break down over time, producing yellowing and brittleness. Acid-free paper is not necessarily permanent: it may still contain lignin or acids that develop over time.

An organic polymer in wood pulp paper that breaks down over time to produce acids. Paper described only as 'acid-free' may still contain lignin and will become acidic as lignin degrades. Archival or 'lignin-free' paper is both acid-free and lignin-free.
A reserve of calcium carbonate added to paper during manufacture to neutralise acids that develop over time. Buffered paper maintains its pH for longer than unbuffered acid-free paper.

What really needs to be archival

Materials that touch original photographs must be archival quality. That means: the album pages, any sleeves or pockets around photographs, photo corners, and any adhesive that contacts an original. Decorative materials (paper, stickers, ribbon, stamps) matter less when they stay separate from the originals. If originals sit in photo corners on an archival page, the rest of the page can use ordinary materials.

Adhesive chemistry matters more than paper chemistry for long-term stability. PVA (polyvinyl acetate) is the conservation standard: acid-free, stays flexible, and can be softened with moisture if you need to remove it. Double-sided tape sold as scrapbooking tape varies widely. Some is truly archival; most is not. Check that any tape is tested to conservation standards before using it near originals. Rubber cement and solvent glues are unsuitable for any archival use. Glue sticks work for decorative elements but not for anything touching irreplaceable photographs.
Storage conditions matter as much as materials

Even the best archival materials deteriorate faster in poor conditions. Photographs and albums stored in attics or garages, where temperature and humidity cycle through extremes, will degrade in decades rather than centuries. Dark, cool, stable conditions protect materials as much as the acid-free specification on the paper itself. Aim for 18 to 20°C and 30 to 50% relative humidity. A bedroom wardrobe or a dedicated archival box in a temperature-controlled room both work well.
